content.title: About
content.content: Green beans, cooked by boiling, are a popular side dish in restaurants. They have a tender flavor, a mildly sweet aroma, and a crisp texture when not overcooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are rich in antioxidants such as vitamin C and flavonoids.
They are used worldwide in salads, soups, and as a stand‑alone side.
The fiber content in cooked beans supports a healthy gut microbiome.
In the United States, green beans are often served with almonds or bacon in classic dishes.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: Cooked green beans provide plant‑based protein that helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: High oxalate levels can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Possible gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause bloating and gas, especially if not chewed thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Green beans can be served as a side, added to salads, soups, stews, or used in cold appetizers. They are often seasoned with salt, lemon juice, or lightly sautéed with garlic.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked green beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in sealed bags.
